claims.claim: Olley says Kay's books are so closely inspired by real events that he sometimes seems not to rewrite history but to write around it.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, University of Oxford Podcasts, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: not to rewrite history but to write around it

claims.claim: Olley attributes Kay's unique style and tone to his ability to find power in quiet moments as well as in brash heroic or sweeping romantic ones.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, University of Oxford Podcasts, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: ability to find power in these quiet moments

claims.claim: Olley says the shift from prose into verse allows a change of register, usually into something more melancholic or portentous.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', University of Oxford Podcasts video lecture, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: By allowing for a change in register

claims.claim: Olley says the verse lament that closes The Lions of Al-Rassan heightens the pathos of the moment and lets Kay impart a sense of closure.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', 16 December 2020
claims.quote: heightens the pathos of the moment

claims.claim: Olley says that in Kay the conclusion of a novel's themes is conveyed not just in content but also in form.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', 16 December 2020
claims.quote: not just what Kaye writes, but how he writes it

claims.claim: Olley says Kay uses a snatch of song at the moment his characters arrive in the other world to signpost a major shift in setting and tone without moving them out of the room.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Verse and Prose in Fantasy Literature', 16 December 2020
claims.quote: A major shift in setting and tone

claims.claim: Hatch reports that the narrator of Sailing to Sarantium states on its first page that writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth.
claims.source: Jillian Hatch, 'The Creative Construction of History in Guy Gavriel Kay's The Sarantine Mosaic', 2005, BrightWeavings Student Papers
claims.quote: writers of history often seek the dramatic over the truth

claims.claim: Hatch argues that Kay's Sarantine narrative is not organised chronologically but cyclically, so that it creates a sense of cause and effect in history rather than a timeline of historical events.
claims.quote: rather than a timeline of historical events

claims.claim: Hatch notes that the Sarantine narrative incorporates flashbacks and often uses several focalizers to emphasise a single event.
claims.quote: often uses several focalizers to emphasize an event

claims.claim: Hatch writes that Kay's Sarantine narrative is focused on the affairs of leaders as well as those of the common man, which she calls a lack of traditional historical emphasis.
claims.quote: as well as those of the

claims.claim: Hatch argues that Kay's fictional historian Pertennius chooses to substantiate rumour while ignoring or twisting things he knows to be fact.
Hatch quotes Lord of Emperors to the effect that historians shape, in years to come, an impression of truth for those who never knew the people written about.
claims.source: Jillian Hatch quoting Kay, Lord of Emperors p.193, BrightWeavings Student Papers, 2005
claims.quote: an impression of truth for those who had never actually known

claims.claim: Aardse reads a Tigana passage in which an elegant tavern in Stevanien is characterised by which travellers are cordially greeted and which are forbidden to enter.
claims.source: Kent Aardse, 'Postcolonialism in Guy Kay's Tigana', undergraduate paper, University of Lethbridge, 2008, hosted at BrightWeavings
claims.quote: no one from Lower Corte was allowed to dine there

claims.claim: Aardse notes that in Tigana the conquered province must be named Lower Corte, after the bitterest of its ancient enemies among the provinces.
claims.source: Kent Aardse, University of Lethbridge, 2008, hosted at BrightWeavings
claims.quote: after the bitterest of our ancient enemies among the provinces

claims.claim: Aardse quotes Kay to the effect that the vengeance in Tigana encompassed names and memory, the fabric of identity, going deeper than occupation and burning and rubble and death.
claims.source: Kent Aardse, University of Lethbridge, 2008, hosted at BrightWeavings
claims.quote: It encompasses names and memory, the fabric of identity
